title: Classes and instances (reference-type blueprints)
hook: A class is a blueprint you write once. When you call `new`, the Common Language Runtime (CLR) creates one object on the managed heap and your variable holds a reference to it — not a copy of the object itself.

blocks.text: A **class** is a reference type: a named blueprint that describes what data and behavior an object can have. The blueprint itself is not the object — you create an object with `new MyClass()`. The variable stores a **reference** (think: a pointer to the object's location), so two variables can point at the same object and see each other's changes.

entries.plainDefinition: A reference-type blueprint that defines fields, properties, methods, and other members. Objects are created from a class with `new`.
entries.example: `public class Customer { }` is the blueprint; `new Customer()` is one customer object.

entries.plainDefinition: A single object created from a class. Each instance has its own field values but shares the same method definitions.
entries.example: `var a = new QueueLease("msg-1");` — `a` is an instance of `QueueLease`.

entries.plainDefinition: The .NET runtime that allocates objects, enforces types, and runs your compiled code.
entries.example: When you call `new`, the CLR allocates memory on the managed heap.

entries.plainDefinition: A value that points to an object on the heap rather than holding the object's data directly.
entries.example: Assigning `b = a` copies the reference, not the object.

blocks.text: Most services you build — an SQS message handler, a Redis connection wrapper, an auth token validator — are classes. They have **identity**: callers share one instance and its lifetime. If you need a snapshot that won't change when someone else mutates the original, you must copy data explicitly (or use a value type like a struct, covered later in this module).

blocks.title: Default visibility
blocks.body: A top-level class defaults to `internal` (visible only inside the same assembly). Members inside a class default to `private`. You choose `public` when other assemblies need to see the type.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Declare the class
items.body: Write the type definition with fields, properties, methods, and constructors. This compiles into metadata — no object exists yet.

items.title: Call `new`
items.body: The CLR allocates memory on the managed heap and runs the constructor to set initial field values.

items.title: Store the reference
items.body: Your variable holds a reference to the heap object. Assignment between variables copies that reference, not the object's data.

items.title: Mutate through any reference
items.body: Changing a property through one variable is visible through every other variable that references the same object.

snippet.label: Two variables, one object
snippet.explanation: Line 1: primary constructor captures `messageId`. Line 8: `new` creates one heap object. Line 9: `b = a` copies the reference. Line 10: mutation through `b` is visible through `a` because both names point at the same object.

snippet.label: Nested type keeps helpers private
snippet.explanation: Line 5: a nested class lives inside another type. It is a way to group helper logic without exposing `Validator` on the assembly's public surface.

snippet.label: When to pick a class over a struct
snippet.explanation: Line 2: `SqsConsumerHost` is a class because it represents a long-lived service with identity. Line 9: `Point` is a struct because it is small data you want to copy by value.

blocks.title: Classes in C# vs JS/TS
rows: Copies the reference to the heap object
Same for objects: `const b = a` aliases the object
Primitives (`number`, `string`) copy; no user-defined value types
TS `private` is compile-time only; JS `#field` is runtime but not metadata
Single base class; `sealed` blocks further inheritance

blocks.title: Assignment does not clone
blocks.body: `var copy = original` does not create a new object when `original` is a class. Both variables reference the same heap object. If you need an independent copy, you must write a clone method or create a new instance with the same values.

blocks.title: Public mutable fields as dictionary keys
blocks.body: A public mutable class used as a dictionary key will break lookups when someone changes a field that affects equality. Keep fields private and design equality deliberately (module 05).

interviewTakeaways: A class variable holds a reference; assignment copies the reference, not the object.
Default type visibility is internal; default member visibility is private.
Choose a class for identity, shared lifetime, and inheritance; choose a struct for small copied data.
commonPitfalls: Assuming `var copy = original` clones a class instance.
Leaving a public mutable class as an implicit DTO and then using it as a dictionary key.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript objects are also reference-like: `const b = a` copies the reference. There is no struct equivalent; primitives are copied. C# makes the split explicit in the type declaration.
A TypeScript class emits a constructor function. A C# class emits CLR metadata and a heap object with a method table. `private` in C# is enforced at run time, not erased.
